transcript.text: Hi, my Bosch WAN28281GB has stopped half way through a wash and is showing E18. Water still in the drum. What does that mean?

E18 on a Bosch washing machine is a drain fault: the machine tried to pump the water out and it either didn't go or took too long, so it stopped and locked out. That fits the water still sitting in the drum. Most likely causes, in order:
1. A blocked pump filter, or something like a coin, hair grip or small sock caught in it or in the pump just behind. This is by far the most common cause and a free fix.
2. A kinked drain hose, or a blockage where it empties (the standpipe or sink waste trap), especially if the machine has been moved recently.
3. Less often, the drain pump itself jammed or failed. Only worth considering once the first two are ruled out. Here's what to do, simplest first: 1. Make it safe and drain the water. Switch off and unplug. Lay plenty of towels down and find a shallow tray or baking dish, as there could be a lot of water. The pump filter is usually behind a small flap at the bottom front. Many Bosch machines also have a small emergency drain hose beside the filter. If yours has one, pull it out, take the cap off and let it drain into the tray in batches. If there's no hose, unscrew the filter only a little at a time and let the water trickle out slowly. 2. Clean the filter. Once the water stops, unscrew the filter fully, clean off any lint or debris and rinse it. If you find something in it, that's very likely your culprit. 3. Check the impeller. With the filter out, shine a torch into the opening and gently turn the small plastic vanes with a finger. They should turn freely, with a slight knock now and then. If they're jammed, broken, or have something wrapped round them, that points at the pump. 4. Check the drain hose at the back. Look for kinks or crushing, especially if the machine was pushed back recently. Also check that the standpipe or sink waste it goes into isn't blocked. 5. Test it. Refit the filter firmly so it doesn't leak, plug back in and run a rinse-and-spin or drain programme. Listen near the bottom front: water should pump away within a minute or two. If it drains after that, you're sorted. If the filter and hose are clear but it still won't drain, tell me whether you can hear the pump humming or whether it's silent. That's what separates a jammed or failed pump from an electrical fault, and tells us whether it's a part you can sensibly replace or an engineer job. To start with, what do you find when you ope

Thanks, that's helpful. I'll unplug it and get towels and a tray ready. The water is still in the drum and I can hear a hum from low down at the front when it tries to drain. I'll open the flap at the bottom front now and let you know what I find.

It means the machine is powering the drain pump, so an electrical or control fault is unlikely. 1. Something is blocking the filter or wrapped round the impeller, such as lint, a coin, a hair grip or a sock.
2. The drain hose or the waste it empties into is blocked or kinked.
3. Less often, the pump itself is jammed or worn. A humming pump doesn't mean it needs replacing, because a simple blockage makes exactly the same sound. 1. Let the water out slowly, using the little emergency hose if there is one or unscrewing the filter a bit at a time. There may be more water than the tray holds, so be ready to stop and empty it.
2. Once the filter is out, look into the opening with a torch and turn the impeller vanes gently with a finger. If they turn freely, with just a slight knock now and then, the pump is probably fine. If they're stiff, jammed or have something wound round them, that's very likely your culprit. If you clear something out, refit the filter firmly and run a drain or spin programme. Let me know what you find: whether the filter was clear, whether you removed something, whether there's a blockage you can't shift, or whether anything looks broken. Tell me too whether the impeller turns freely.

Right, I've got the water out using the little emergency hose, it took several trays and the water was grey and smelled a bit. I've unscrewed the filter and there was a child's sock and a hair grip wrapped round it, plus a lot of fluff. I'll check the impeller next. A bit of the floor got wet while I was draining it, but no water near the socket.

A child's sock and a hair grip wrapped round the filter is probably your E18. The grey, slightly smelly water is normal for wash water that's been sitting in the drum, so nothing to worry about there. 1. Look into the filter opening with a torch and pick out any remaining fluff or threads. A sock can leave fibres wound round the impeller.
2. Turn the impeller vanes gently with a finger. Free turning with an occasional slight knock is normal and means the pump is fine. Stiff, jammed or chipped vanes (the hair grip can sometimes damage them) would point to the pump.
3. Rinse the filter, check its rubber seal is clean and not damaged, then screw it back in fully and straight. A filter that isn't seated properly is the usual cause of a drip after this job.
4. Wipe up the floor and make sure everything is dry. Then plug in and run a rinse-and-spin or drain programme. Listen at the bottom front and keep an eye on the flap for drips. If it pumps away within a minute or two and the code doesn't come back, you're sorted. If it still hums but won't drain with the impeller turning freely, check the drain hose at the back for kinks and make sure the standpipe or sink waste isn't blocked. Only after that would the pump itself be the likely part. Let me know how the impeller feels and whether it drains.
I checked the impeller with the power off and it turns, slightly notchy at first and then free. I'll clean the filter, put it back in and run a drain/spin programme, then let you know.

That impeller sounds healthy. Most drain pumps use a magnetic rotor, so a slight notchy or cogging feel for the first bit of a turn, then turning freely, is normal. So the sock and hair grip remain by far the most likely cause of the E18, and the pump itself looks fine for now. 1. Screw the filter in fully and straight, with the seal clean. Close the flap and plug back in.
2. If E18 is still showing, switch off at the dial or button, wait a few seconds, then switch back on. Then select a drain or spin programme.
3. Listen at the bottom front. You should hear the pump and water rushing away within a minute or two. That means it's fixed.
4. Keep an eye on the filter flap and the floor during the spin. A drip there almost always means the filter isn't quite seated, so unplug it and screw it in again. If it still hums but won't drain, check the drain hose at the back for kinks and the standpipe or sink waste for a blockage. If those are clear, the next suspects are sock fibres lodged further back in the sump hose or pump housing, or a weak pump. Both are engineer-level jobs, as they mean taking the machine apart. Once it's draining, an empty hot wash (60°C or a drum-clean programme) will help clear the smell left by the standing water. Let me know how the test goes.
I've refilled and run the drain/spin programme after cleaning the filter. It drains quickly, E18 has gone and it spins normally now. Thanks!

That's sorted, then. The sock and hair grip in the filter were the cause of the E18. It's draining quickly, the code has cleared and it spins normally, so the pump is clearly fine too. 1. Wash small items like children's socks in a mesh laundry bag, and check pockets for hair grips, coins and tissues before loading.
2. Clean the pump filter every couple of months. 3. Run an empty hot wash (60°C or a drum-clean programme) soon, to clear the smell from the standing water.
4. Over the next wash or two, glance at the filter flap and the floor. A drip there usually just means the filter needs screwing in a little more firmly and straight. Is there anything else I can help with?
